problems.prompt: What distinguishes the Meissner effect from a material simply being a perfect conductor (zero resistance)?
choices: The superconductor actively expels an existing field, whereas a perfect conductor would only freeze in whatever field was present when it became resistance-free
They are exactly the same phenomenon
A perfect conductor expels fields but a superconductor does not
The Meissner effect only applies above T_c
problems.explain: Zero resistance alone would trap (freeze) any pre-existing field. The Meissner effect actively pushes the field out of the bulk below T_c, regardless of field history — a distinct, stronger statement about the superconducting phase.

problems.prompt: At depth x = λ_L (one London penetration depth) inside the superconductor, the field has dropped to ____ of its surface value B_0.
problems.explain: B(λ_L) = B_0 e^(−λ_L/λ_L) = B_0/e ≈ 0.368 B_0, about 37% of the surface value.

problems.prompt: Why does the small magnet levitate above the puck when T<T_c but rest directly on it when T≥T_c?
choices: Below T_c the puck expels the magnet's field and the resulting screening currents repel the magnet; above T_c the puck is normal and the field passes through with no repulsion
The puck becomes heavier above T_c
Levitation is caused by air pressure, unrelated to temperature
The magnet's field reverses direction above T_c
problems.explain: Diamagnetic repulsion from the Meissner screening currents supports the magnet's weight only while the puck is superconducting; once T ≥ T_c the field simply penetrates and there is no repulsive force.

problems.prompt: If B_0 = 20 mT and λ_L = 150 nm, what is B(x) at depth x = 300 nm (T<T_c)? Use B(x) = B_0 e^(−x/λ_L).
